primary_claim: Across 14 evaluated models, every reasoning model except Claude sometimes produces illegible chain-of-thought segments; restricting a model to only the legible portions of its CoT increases incorrect answers by 36% (showing the illegible text is useful to the model), illegibility increases on harder questions, yet across many resampled responses to the same question there is no meaningful correlation (r=0.061) between per-sample CoT illegibility and answer correctness, suggesting illegible reasoning is not more effective than legible natural-language reasoning.

effect.metric: illegibility score (1-10); accuracy drop when restricted to legible CoT prefix; correlation between illegibility and correctness
effect.value: with the exception of Claude, every reasoning model sometimes produces illegible CoTs; forcing QwQ to answer using only the legible prefix increases incorrect answers by 36%; correlation between per-sample illegibility and correctness across resampled responses is near zero (r=0.061)

limitations_stated: The complex-steganography hypothesis seems unlikely given the near-zero correlation between illegibility and performance, though this doesn't rule out models finding some narrower use for the illegible tokens.
If most illegible tokens are useless but a monitor cannot reliably distinguish the useful subset from noise, this doesn't actually help monitoring.
The 36% performance-drop estimate is confounded by expected degradation from going off-policy when prefilling with a truncated, legible-only CoT.
quote: With the exception of Claude, every reasoning model sometimes produces illegible CoTs, always returning legible text afterward.
